docs.title: Users, packages and the environment
docs.text:
What you need first

Moving around the filesystem and running commands, from The shell and the filesystem.

docs.title: Three questions every system answers
docs.text:
When you run a program on a Unix system, three things decide what happens before your code does anything at all:

  1. Who is running it? The user determines which files the program can read, write or execute.
  2. What is installed? The program can only use the tools and libraries that are on the system, in the versions that are there.
  3. What is its environment? A set of named values, the environment variables, tells it where to find things and how to behave.

These are layers 2, 3 and 6 of the environment stack from session 1. This page covers each one.

docs.title: Users and groups
docs.text:
Unix was designed for many people sharing one machine, so every file and every running program belongs to a user. Users are collected into groups, which let several users share access. The id command shows who you are:

id

uid=1000(ana) gid=1000(ana) groups=1000(ana),4(adm),27(sudo),...

You are the user ana, with number (uid) 1000, and you belong to several groups, including sudo (more on that below). There is also one special user, root (uid 0), the administrator, who can read, change and delete anything.

Servers also have users that are not people. A database server runs as user postgres, a web server as www-data. If one of them is compromised, the attacker gets only that user's permissions, not the whole machine. You will see the same idea in session 11: well-built containers don't run as root.

docs.title: Reading permissions
docs.text:
ls -l shows who owns each file and what everyone may do with it. Here is a ledger folder like the one from Lab 2, with an extra private folder, and two system files:

$ ls -l ~/smd/ledger
drwxr-xr-x  2 ana  ana   4096 Oct 29 10:02 data
-rwxr-xr-x  1 ana  ana    252 Oct 29 10:05 balance.sh
-rw-r--r--  1 ana  ana    180 Oct 29 10:07 report.txt
drwx------  2 ana  ana   4096 Oct 29 10:08 private
$ ls -l /etc/passwd /etc/shadow
-rw-r--r--  1 root root    888 Oct 24 14:12 /etc/passwd
-rw-r-----  1 root shadow  502 Oct 24 14:12 /etc/shadow

The first column has ten characters. The first says what the entry is (- a file, d a directory, l a link). The other nine are three groups of three, for three kinds of people:

 -   rwx   r-x   r-x
     │     │     └── others: everyone else
     │     └──────── group: members of the file's group (the second name)
     └────────────── owner: the file's user (the first name)

In each group, r is permission to read, w to write and x to execute (run the file as a program; for a directory, to enter it). A - means the permission is missing.

On a folder the same letters mean slightly different things: r lets you list what is inside, w lets you create, rename and delete files in it, and x lets you enter it with cd. A folder with drwx------ is private: nobody but its owner can even look inside.

So balance.sh can be read, changed and run by ana, and read and run by everyone else. report.txt can be changed only by ana, and private is a folder nobody else can enter. /etc/passwd (the list of users) is readable by everybody but writable only by root. /etc/shadow, which contains the password hashes, cannot even be read by normal users:

cat /etc/shadow

cat: /etc/shadow: Permission denied

Definition: file permissions

Each file has an owner and a group, and three sets of permissions: for the owner, for the group and for others. Each set says whether that class of user may read (r), write (w) or execute (x) the file.

docs.title: Changing permissions
docs.text:
chmod (change mode) changes permissions. The readable form says who, + or -, and what:

chmod +x balance.sh      # everyone may execute it
chmod go-r notes.txt     # group and others may no longer read it
chmod u+w report.txt     # the owner (user) may write it

You will also see a numeric form, where each set is a digit: r = 4, w = 2, x = 1, added up. chmod 755 file means rwxr-xr-x (7 = 4+2+1 for the owner, 5 = 4+1 for the others), and chmod 600 key.pem means rw-------: only the owner can read and write. That last one is the standard for files with secrets, such as SSH keys, and SSH refuses to use a private key that others can read.

The most frequent reason to use chmod in this course is a script you have just written. A new file is not executable, so ./balance.sh gives Permission denied until you run chmod +x balance.sh.

With -R (recursive), chmod changes a folder and everything inside it: chmod -R g+w data lets the group write in data and in all its files.

docs.title: Changing the owner
docs.text:
chown (change owner) gives a file to another user, and optionally another group, written user:group:

sudo chown ana report.txt          # ana becomes the owner
sudo chown ana:staff report.txt    # owner ana, group staff
sudo chown -R ana:ana data         # the folder and everything inside it

Giving a file away needs sudo, explained next: otherwise any user could hand files to someone else. You'll use chown mostly to repair files that were created as root by mistake, for example by running a command with sudo that didn't need it, and that your own user now can't change.

docs.title: sudo
docs.text:
Installing software or changing system configuration requires root. Instead of logging in as root, you run single commands with sudo (superuser do). Without it, installing fails because a normal user can't write to the system folders:

$ apt install tree
E: Could not open lock file /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend - open (13: Permission denied)
E: Unable to acquire the dpkg frontend lock (/var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend), are you root?
$ sudo apt install tree
[sudo] password for ana:

sudo asks for your password (not root's), checks that your user is allowed (on Ubuntu, membership of the sudo group; on macOS, of admin) and runs that one command as root. Every use is logged.

This applies the principle of least privilege: work as a normal user, and become root only for the command that needs it. A typo in a normal command can damage your files; the same typo with sudo can damage the whole system. Don't put sudo in front of a command just because it failed. Find out why it failed first. The answer is often a wrong path, not a missing permission.

docs.title: Installing software: package managers
docs.text:
On Windows, people traditionally install software by downloading an installer from a website. Unix systems use a package manager instead: a program that downloads software from trusted repositories, installs it in the standard places, installs whatever else it depends on, and can update or remove all of it later with one command.

System Package manager Install Update everything Ubuntu, Debian (and WSL) apt sudo apt install tree sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade macOS Homebrew (brew) brew install tree brew update && brew upgrade Windows winget winget install Git.Git winget upgrade --all

With apt, sudo apt update refreshes the list of available packages and their versions from the repositories. It doesn't install anything. sudo apt upgrade installs the new versions. Run update before installing anything on a machine you haven't used for a while, or apt may try to download versions that no longer exist.

Homebrew installs into its own folder (/opt/homebrew on Apple Silicon) and doesn't need sudo.

Package managers solve the same problem at the system level that the lockfiles of session 4 solve for a project: known versions, installed in a repeatable way, from a trusted source. You can write down a list of packages and anyone can install exactly that list.

Install from trusted sources

A package manager verifies that what it downloads comes from the repository it claims to come from. A random installer or script from the web has no such check. When documentation tells you to run curl … | sh (download a script and run it immediately), it is executing code you haven't read with your user's permissions. Do it only for well-known projects, from their official site.

docs.title: What they are
docs.text:
Every running program receives a set of named text values from whoever started it: its environment variables. Programs read them to find out where things are and how to behave. Some are always there:

echo $HOME      # your home directory
echo $USER      # your user name
echo $SHELL     # your shell
env             # all of them

The $ in front of a name asks the shell to replace it with the variable's value. By convention, environment variable names are in capitals.

Definition: environment variable

An environment variable is a named text value (NAME=value) that a process receives when it starts. A child process inherits a copy of its parent's variables. Changes in the child never affect the parent.

docs.title: Setting them
docs.text:
There are three ways, with different scopes:

LEDGER_FILE=data/checking.csv ./balance.sh   # only for this one command
export LEDGER_FILE=data/checking.csv         # for this shell and everything it starts afterwards
unset LEDGER_FILE                            # remove it

A variable set with export disappears when you close the terminal. To make it permanent, add the export line to your shell's startup file: ~/.zshrc for zsh, ~/.bashrc for bash. The shell reads that file every time it starts.

This is how Ana's script in session 1 got its RISK_THRESHOLD: an export line in her ~/.zshrc that nobody else had. Environment variables are the standard way to configure software, especially in containers and in the cloud. Session 12 shows how to manage them so that this can't happen to you.

docs.title: PATH: how the shell finds commands
docs.text:
When you type python3, how does the shell know which program to run? It looks in the folders listed in the PATH variable, in order, and runs the first python3 it finds:

echo $PATH | tr ":" "\n"

/usr/local/sbin
/usr/local/bin
/usr/sbin
/usr/bin
/sbin
/bin

(tr ":" "\n" replaces the colons with line breaks so the list is readable.) which tells you which file a command name resolves to:

which python3

Two everyday errors come from PATH:

  • command not found right after installing something. The program was installed in a folder that isn't in PATH. The installer usually says which folder and how to add it. Often you just need to open a new terminal, so that the shell reads its updated startup file.
  • The wrong version runs. You have two Pythons, and the one that comes first in PATH isn't the one you expected. which python3 and python3 --version tell you which one you're getting.

That is also why we ran ./balance.sh and not balance.sh. The current folder isn't in PATH (for security), so a program in it must be called with an explicit path.

docs.title: Processes
docs.text:
Every running program is a process, with a number (PID), an owner and its own environment. A few commands are enough to start with:

Command Does ps aux lists all processes top or htop live view of processes and their CPU and memory use (Q to quit) kill PID asks a process to stop (kill -9 PID forces it) cmd & runs cmd in the background, giving you the prompt back

You will need these when a server you started in one terminal keeps a port busy, or a program hangs.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• sudo as a reflex. It hides the real problem and can create files owned by root in your home folder, which then cause more Permission denied errors. Use it only for installing software and changing the system.
  • chmod 777 "to make it work". It gives every user write permission. It's never the right fix, especially for files with secrets.
  • Spaces around =. NAME = value is an error in the shell; it must be NAME=value.
  • Forgetting export. NAME=value alone (on its own line) sets a shell variable that the programs you start don't see. Use export NAME=value, or put the assignment in front of the command.
  • Editing PATH and losing the old value. Write export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH", which adds a folder, never export PATH="$HOME/bin", which replaces the whole list.

Key takeaways

  • Every file has an owner, a group and rwx permissions for owner, group and others. chmod changes them, and chmod +x makes a script runnable.
  • root can do anything. Work as a normal user and use sudo only for the single commands that need it (least privilege).
  • Package managers (apt, brew, winget) install software from trusted repositories, with its dependencies, in a repeatable way.
  • Environment variables configure programs and are inherited by child processes. Set them for one command (NAME=x cmd), for a session (export) or permanently (~/.zshrc, ~/.bashrc).
  • PATH lists where the shell looks for commands. which shows what a name resolves to, and most command not found errors are PATH problems.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Decode these permissions and say who can do what: (a) -rw-r--r-- owned by ana; (b) -rwx------; (c) drwxr-x--- owned by ana, group finance.

Solution
  • (a) A file that ana can read and write, and that everyone else can only read. This is the usual default for a new file.
  • (b) A file that only its owner can read, write and execute. Nobody else can do anything with it: typical for a private script.
  • (c) A directory (the d). ana can list it, create files in it and enter it. Members of finance can list it and enter it, but not create or delete files. Others can't even enter it.

2. Write the numeric chmod for: (a) rwxr-xr-x; (b) rw-------; (c) rw-r-----.

Solution

Add up r = 4, w = 2, x = 1 in each group of three:

  • (a) 7, 5, 5 → chmod 755
  • (b) 6, 0, 0 → chmod 600
  • (c) 6, 4, 0 → chmod 640

3. You install a tool following its instructions, but typing its name gives command not found. The installer printed "installed to ~/.local/bin". What is happening, and how do you fix it?

Solution

The shell looks for commands only in the folders listed in PATH, and ~/.local/bin isn't one of them. First, open a new terminal: many installers add the folder to your startup file, and only new shells read it. If it still fails, check with echo $PATH | tr ":" "\n". If the folder is missing, add export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" at the end of ~/.zshrc (or ~/.bashrc) and open a new terminal.

4. In one terminal you run export API_KEY=abc123. In a second terminal window, echo $API_KEY prints an empty line. Why?

Solution

An environment variable belongs to a process and is inherited only by the processes it starts. Each terminal window runs a separate shell, and neither is a child of the other, so the second one never received the variable. To have it in every shell you would put the export in your startup file. For a secret like an API key, though, that's a bad idea: session 12 shows better ways.

5. In the lab, balance.sh ends with awk … "$file" | sort. When LEDGER_FILE points to a file that doesn't exist, awk prints an error, but echo $? right after shows 0. Why? Why does it matter?

Solution

The exit code of a pipeline is the exit code of its last command. awk failed, but sort successfully sorted its empty input and returned 0. That matters because automated tools (scripts, CI pipelines, schedulers) decide whether a step worked by its exit code. This script would report success while producing nothing, which is Ana's dangerous kind of failure again. In bash, set -o pipefail at the top of a script makes a pipeline fail if any of its commands fails. It is a good habit, together with set -e (stop at the first failing command) and set -u (treat an undefined variable as an error).

docs.title: Python projects with uv
docs.text:
Most people learn Python in a notebook: open it, pip install whatever is missing, run the cells. That is fine for exploring data, and it is exactly how you get Ana's "works on my machine" problem from session 1. Software that a team builds, tests and deploys needs more. It needs a known Python version, its own environment and a standard way to run it. This session sets that up with uv: a single, fast tool that manages Python versions, virtual environments and projects.

By the end, ledger is a Python project with its own Python and environment, ready for its code. You write the code, and add the project's first dependency, in session 4.

docs.title: The thread of the session
docs.text:
1. Python projects and environments. What the interpreter is and what Python versions mean for compatibility. Where installed packages go, why every project needs its own virtual environment, and what pyproject.toml declares.
  2. Lab 3: the ledger becomes a Python project. You install uv and a specific Python, create the ledger project, run it in its own environment, and see requires-python refuse an older Python.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of the session you should be able to:

  • Explain what the Python interpreter does, and what a project's requires-python protects against.
  • Explain what a virtual environment is, why each project needs its own, and how uv run uses it.
  • Read the [project] and [project.scripts] sections of a pyproject.toml.
  • Install a Python version with uv, create a project with uv init and run it with uv run.

docs.text: You need the course environment from session 2 and the ~/smd/ledger folder from Lab 2. If you didn't finish Lab 2, the start of Lab 3 has the two commands that create the folder and download the data. Basic Python is assumed: variables, lists, dictionaries, loops and functions. If you need a refresher, the official Python tutorial (sections 3 to 5) covers it.

docs.title: Lab 3: the ledger becomes a Python project
docs.text:
What you need first

The course environment from session 2 and the folder ~/smd/ledger with data/transactions.csv from Lab 2. The concepts are in Python projects and environments.

If you didn't finish Lab 2

This lab only needs the data file from Lab 2. These commands create the folder and download the file:

mkdir -p ~/smd/ledger/data
cd ~/smd/ledger
curl -fsSL -o data/transactions.csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ami232/ie-smd/main/data/transactions.csv

ls data should show transactions.csv. Finish the rest of Lab 2 at home.

In Lab 2, balance.sh answered one question with awk. In this lab you turn ~/smd/ledger into a Python project: a pinned Python version, its own virtual environment and a command called ledger. In Lab 4 you write the code of that command.

Work in the course shell (the macOS Terminal, the Ubuntu terminal in WSL, the VM or the codespace).

docs.title: 1. Install uv
docs.text:
macOSLinux, WSL, VM, codespace 
brew install uv

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

The installer puts uv in ~/.local/bin and adds that folder to your PATH in your shell's startup file. Open a new terminal (or run source $HOME/.local/bin/env) so the shell sees it.

Then check:

uv --version
What you should see

A line such as uv 0.13.6. Any recent version works. If you get command not found, it is the PATH problem from session 2: open a new terminal.

If your prompt starts with (base): conda

If you installed Anaconda or Miniconda, your prompt may start with (base). This means conda's base environment is active in every terminal, so python3 and pip are conda's. In the next steps you compare the system Python with the project's Python, and with conda active the results are confusing. VS Code may also suggest conda's Python instead of the project's. Turn it off for this course:

conda deactivate
conda config --set auto_activate_base false

The first command turns it off in this terminal. The second stops it from turning on in new terminals (if conda says the setting is deprecated, use conda config --set auto_activate false). Conda stays installed, and conda activate base turns it on when you need it. Open a new terminal: the (base) should be gone.

docs.title: 2. Install a Python version
docs.text:
First, see what your system already has:

python3 --version
which python3

This is the system Python: the one your operating system uses for its own tools. It may be missing, or a different version on each machine (Ubuntu 24.04 comes with 3.12; macOS may have none, or the 3.9 from Apple's developer tools). Don't rely on it for projects. Ask uv for the exact version we use instead:

uv python install 3.14
uv python list --only-installed
What you should see

uv downloads a standalone build of Python 3.14 (about 30 MB) and reports something like Installed Python 3.14.10. The list shows it next to any Python your system already had. uv keeps its own Pythons in its own folder and never touches the system one.

docs.title: 3. Create the project
docs.text:
Go into the ledger folder and turn it into a project:

cd ~/smd/ledger
uv init --package --vcs none --python 3.14
  • --package creates an installable package with a command-line entry point (not just a script).
  • --vcs none skips creating a Git repository. We do that properly in session 5.
  • --python 3.14 pins the project to Python 3.14.

Look at what it created, including hidden files:

ls -a
cat pyproject.toml
cat .python-version
cat src/ledger/__init__.py
What you should see

docs.title: Python projects and environments
docs.text:
What you need first

The layers of an environment and the idea of reproducibility, from Environments and reproducibility. Environment variables and PATH, from Users, packages and the environment.

docs.title: From a script to a project
docs.text:
Ana's fraud script from session 1 was a script: one file, run by hand, depending on whatever happened to be installed on her laptop. Scripts are great for exploring. Once other people need to run the code, though, on other machines and for months, it becomes a project, and it needs four things the script didn't have:

  1. A declared Python version, so nobody runs it on an interpreter that can't understand it.
  2. Its own set of installed libraries, separate from those of every other project on the machine.
  3. A precise list of those libraries and their versions, so that every installation is identical.
  4. A standard way to run it, documented in the project itself.

This page explains the version, the environment and the way to run it, and the lab builds them with uv. The precise list of libraries comes with the project's first dependency, in session 4.

docs.title: The interpreter
docs.text:
When you run python3 report.py, the program python3 is the interpreter. It reads your source code, translates it into an intermediate form called bytecode and executes it, instruction by instruction. The standard interpreter, the one you download from python.org or that uv installs, is called CPython because it is written in C.

This is different from languages like C, Go or Rust, which are compiled: a compiler turns the source code into machine code for one processor and one operating system before it runs, and you distribute the result. Python code, by contrast, is distributed as source, and it runs wherever there is a suitable interpreter. That makes the interpreter itself part of the environment, with two consequences:

  • The interpreter must be installed on every machine that runs the code. A container image for a Python application (session 11) always starts from an image that already has Python.
  • Its version matters, because each version understands a slightly different language.

docs.title: Python versions
docs.text:
Python versions have the form 3.14.2: major, minor and patch numbers. Python has been at major version 3 since 2008. A new minor version comes out every October, adding features to the language and to the standard library. Each one receives bug fixes and then security fixes for five years, after which it reaches its end of life. Patch versions (3.14.1, 3.14.2…) only fix bugs and never change the language.

Code is forward compatible within major version 3, with few exceptions: code written for 3.10 almost always runs on 3.14. The reverse is not true. Code that uses something new fails on older versions:

Feature Since What happens on an older Python match statement 3.10 SyntaxError before anything runs tomllib module (read TOML files) 3.11 ModuleNotFoundError type aliases (type Amount = Decimal) 3.12 SyntaxError

That is why a project declares the oldest Python it supports, with requires-python = ">=3.14" in its configuration. Tools refuse to install the project on anything older, so the error happens at installation with a clear message, not in production with a confusing one.

Which version should a new project use? Usually the newest one that all your libraries support. A brand-new Python version takes a few months to be supported by every library that includes compiled code, so professional teams often stay one version behind the newest during its first months. In this course we use Python 3.14.

docs.title: Imports and site-packages
docs.text:
When Python runs import pandas, it searches a list of folders, sys.path, for a module or package called pandas. One of those folders is the interpreter's site-packages, and that is where installing a package puts it. Installing is just downloading a package (usually a wheel, a ready-to-install .whl archive) from the Python Package Index (PyPI, pypi.org) and unpacking it into site-packages.

That works well for one project. Now imagine two projects on the same laptop. Project A was written two years ago with pandas 1.5. Project B is new and needs pandas 2.3. There is only one site-packages per interpreter, so there can be only one pandas. Install 2.3 for project B, and project A breaks. This is the classic dependency conflict, and the more projects you have, the worse it gets.

docs.title: Virtual environments
docs.text:
The solution is to give each project its own site-packages.

Definition: virtual environment

A virtual environment (venv) is a folder, conventionally called .venv inside the project, that contains a link to a Python interpreter and its own empty site-packages. Packages installed in it are visible only to programs that run with that environment's Python, .venv/bin/python.

Inside the venv there is a bin folder with its own python and the command-line programs of the installed packages. Running code "in the environment" just means using that python. There are two ways to do so:

  • Activate the environment: source .venv/bin/activate puts .venv/bin at the front of your PATH (that is all it does), so python now means the venv's Python. deactivate undoes it.
  • Let a tool choose it: uv run report.py finds the project's .venv, creates or updates it if needed, and runs the command with its Python. You never activate anything, so you can't forget to.

A virtual environment is disposable. It is built from the project's files, it is not committed to Git, and if it gets into a strange state you delete it and rebuild it. It is also specific to one machine: it contains absolute paths and, for compiled libraries, code for one operating system and architecture. You never copy a .venv to another computer; you rebuild it there.

docs.title: pyproject.toml
docs.text:
Every modern Python project is described by one file, pyproject.toml, written in the TOML format (sections in [brackets], then key = value lines). This is the one uv init creates in the lab:

[project]
name = "ledger"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = []

[project.scripts]
ledger = "ledger:main"

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.13.6,<0.14.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"
  • [project] holds the standard metadata: the name, the version of your project, the supported Python and the list of direct dependencies. It is empty for now: ledger gets its first dependency in session 4.
  • [project.scripts] creates a command: ledger will run the function main of the package ledger. This is the "standard way to run it" from the start of the page.
  • [build-system] says which tool turns the project into an installable package. You won't need to touch it.

The structure is a standard (it is the same for every tool), so the project doesn't depend on uv: pip and others can read it too.

docs.title: uv
docs.text:
For years, Python developers needed several tools for all this: pyenv to install Python versions, venv or virtualenv for environments, pip to install packages, pip-tools or Poetry for lockfiles, pipx for command-line tools. uv does all of it in one program, and much faster (it is written in Rust). These are the commands for creating and running a project:

Command Does uv python install 3.14 downloads and installs a Python version, independently of the system's uv python list shows the Python versions uv can find, its own and the system's uv init --package creates a project: pyproject.toml, .python-version, src/<name>/ uv run <cmd> runs a command in the project's environment, creating the environment first if needed uv python pin 3.14 changes the project's Python version in .python-version

The file .python-version (just 3.14) tells uv which Python to use for the project's environment, and uv downloads it if it's missing. The commands for adding libraries to a project come in session 4.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using pip install on the system Python. It mixes the packages of every project, and on recent Linux and macOS versions it is refused with an externally-managed-environment error, precisely to prevent this. Install libraries in a project's environment instead.
  • Committing .venv. It is large, specific to one machine and rebuilt in seconds. Commit the files that describe the project (pyproject.toml, .python-version, src/) and ignore .venv.
  • "It works in my notebook." A notebook's kernel may use a completely different Python and packages than your project. If the code is part of the project, run it with uv run.

Key takeaways

  • Python code runs on an interpreter, which is part of the environment. New language features fail on older versions, so a project declares requires-python.
  • Installed packages go into the interpreter's site-packages. A virtual environment gives each project its own, avoiding conflicts. It is disposable and is rebuilt, never copied.
  • pyproject.toml describes the project: its name, the Python it needs (requires-python) and the commands it provides ([project.scripts]).
  • uv installs Python versions, creates projects and runs commands in the project's environment with uv run.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. A colleague's code starts with import tomllib and fails with ModuleNotFoundError on the server, though it works on their laptop. What is the likely cause, and what line in pyproject.toml would have caught it earlier?

Solution

tomllib was added to the standard library in Python 3.11, so the server is running an older Python. If the project declared requires-python = ">=3.11" (or higher), installing it on the server would have failed at once with a clear message about the Python version, instead of failing when the code ran.

2. Explain what source .venv/bin/activate changes, and why uv run ledger works without it.

Solution

Activating only puts .venv/bin at the front of the PATH variable of the current shell, so commands like python or ledger are found in the virtual environment first. uv run doesn't need that, because it finds the project's environment itself (from the pyproject.toml of the current folder or its parents), creates or updates it if needed, and runs the command with it directly.

docs.title: Dependencies and the lockfile
docs.text:
What you need first

Virtual environments, pyproject.toml and the basic uv commands, from Python projects and environments, and the ledger project from Lab 3.

A project needs four things: a declared Python version, its own environment, a standard way to run it, and a precise list of the libraries it uses. The first three were set up in session 3. So far ledger only uses Python's standard library, so the list is empty. The moment it needs a library from PyPI, the project needs that fourth thing, and this page explains how it works.

docs.title: Direct and transitive
docs.text:
The libraries your code imports are its direct dependencies. They have dependencies of their own, which you also need: these are transitive dependencies. In Lab 4, ledger depends on one library, rich, which draws tables in the terminal. But installing it brings four packages:

ledger v0.1.0
└── rich v15.0.0
    ├── markdown-it-py v4.2.0
    │   └── mdurl v0.1.2
    └── pygments v2.21.0

A typical web application has a dozen direct dependencies and a hundred transitive ones. Any of them can change.

docs.title: Version constraints
docs.text:
You declare a direct dependency with a constraint, a range of acceptable versions, such as rich>=15.0.0. Constraints rely on a convention called semantic versioning: in MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, a new major version may break your code, a minor one adds features without breaking anything, and a patch only fixes bugs. Many projects follow it, some loosely.

Constraint Means rich any version rich>=15.0 15.0 or newer, including a future 16.0 that may break things rich>=15.0,<16 any 15.x: features and fixes, no breaking changes rich==15.0.0 exactly that version

Constraints alone are not enough for reproducibility. rich>=15.0 installs today's newest version today and a different one next month, and the same goes for every transitive dependency. Two people installing the "same" project a month apart can get different code.

docs.title: The lockfile
docs.text:
Definition: lockfile

A lockfile records the exact version of every package the project needs, direct and transitive, with a hash of each file to verify the download. It is generated by a tool from the constraints, committed to the repository, and used to install exactly the same packages everywhere.

The two files have different jobs. pyproject.toml says what the project accepts (its constraints). It is written by people. uv.lock says what the project uses (the resolved versions). It is written by the tool. Changing a dependency means editing the constraints, usually with uv add or uv remove, and letting the tool update the lock. When you want newer versions, you upgrade deliberately (uv lock --upgrade), run the tests, and commit the new lockfile, so the change is visible and reviewable.

docs.title: uv commands for dependencies
docs.text:
Command Does uv add rich adds a dependency: updates pyproject.toml, uv.lock and .venv uv add --dev ruff adds a dependency only for development (tests, linters), in its own group uv remove rich removes a dependency uv sync makes .venv match uv.lock exactly (installs, upgrades, removes) uv tree shows the dependency tree uv lock --upgrade resolves again with the newest versions the constraints allow

uv run also syncs the environment before running, so after a teammate changes the lockfile, your next uv run installs what changed. Together, .python-version, pyproject.toml and uv.lock describe layers 4 and 5 of the environment completely. Anyone who has uv can rebuild them identically, which is exactly the "automate it" level of reproducibility from session 1.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Not committing uv.lock. Without it, the project is not reproducible: every installation resolves the constraints again.
  • Editing the lockfile by hand. It is generated. Change the constraints, with uv add or uv remove, and let uv update it.
  • Constraints that are too loose or too tight. With rich alone, any future version is accepted, even one that breaks the code. With rich==15.0.0, the project never gets bug fixes, and it can't be installed next to another library that needs a newer rich. A lower bound such as rich>=15.0.0, which is what uv add writes, plus the lockfile, is the usual choice.

Key takeaways

  • Direct dependencies are the ones your code imports; they bring their own transitive dependencies.
  • pyproject.toml declares the direct dependencies with constraints, a range of acceptable versions. It is written by people.
  • The lockfile, uv.lock, pins every package to an exact version, with hashes. It is written by uv. Commit both files.
  • uv add and uv remove change the constraints and the lockfile together; uv sync makes .venv match the lockfile.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. In the dependency tree above, which dependencies are direct and which transitive? If rich stopped needing pygments in a future version, what would you have to change in pyproject.toml?

Solution

rich is the only direct dependency of ledger. markdown-it-py, mdurl and pygments are transitive: ledger gets them because rich needs them. You wouldn't change anything in pyproject.toml, because pygments is not listed there. After upgrading rich (uv lock --upgrade-package rich), uv would drop pygments from uv.lock, and uv sync would uninstall it from .venv.

2. Your pyproject.toml says pandas>=2.0. Today, uv locks pandas 2.3.3. Six months later a teammate clones the repository. (a) With the lockfile committed, which version does uv sync install for them? (b) And if the lockfile was not committed?

Solution
  • (a) Exactly 2.3.3, the version in uv.lock, whatever is newer on PyPI. That is the point of the lockfile.
  • (b) uv resolves the constraint again, so they get the newest version that satisfies >=2.0 six months later, maybe 2.4 or even a 3.0 that breaks the code. The two of you would be running different code without knowing it.

The ledger project from Lab 3: the folder ~/smd/ledger with pyproject.toml, src/ledger/__init__.py and .venv, where uv run ledger prints Hello from ledger!. The concepts of dependencies are in Dependencies and the lockfile.

docs.title: 1. Set up VS Code
docs.text: From here on you write Python. A plain text editor saves the file, but it doesn't help you write it. Set up VS Code, the editor we use for the rest of the course, and connect it to the project.

docs.title: Install VS Code and the code command
docs.text:
You open projects from the terminal with the code command, so VS Code must be installed and code must be in your PATH.

macOSWindows (WSL) 
brew install --cask visual-studio-code

Homebrew installs the app in Applications and puts code in its own folder of the PATH. If Homebrew says the app already exists, you installed VS Code earlier from a download: keep it, and skip to the check below.

VS Code runs on Windows, not inside Ubuntu. In PowerShell:

winget install -e --id Microsoft.VisualStudioCode

or download the installer from code.visualstudio.com and keep the option Add to PATH checked. Then open VS Code, go to the Extensions view (Ctrl+Shift+X), search for WSL and install the extension by Microsoft. Close VS Code.

With the WSL extension, the VS Code window runs on Windows, and a small server runs inside Ubuntu. The files, Python and uv stay in Linux, where the rest of the course runs.

Now open a new terminal (the Ubuntu terminal on Windows) and check:

code --version
What you should see

Three lines: a version number such as 1.106.0, a long commit identifier and the architecture (arm64 or x64).

If you get command not found, the code command is not in your PATH:

  • macOS, VS Code installed from a download: move Visual Studio Code to the Applications folder if it isn't there, and open it. Open the Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P), type shell command and choose Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH. Open a new terminal and try again.

docs.title: Open the project
docs.text:
cd ~/smd/ledger

. is the current folder: you are telling VS Code to open the folder you are in. VS Code calls an open folder a workspace.

A VS Code window with the project's files in the Explorer on the left: .venv, data, src, .python-version, pyproject.toml, README.md and uv.lock.

  • macOS: VS Code asks Do you trust the authors of the files in this folder? Choose Yes, I trust the authors: they are your own files.

Then open a terminal inside VS Code with Terminal → New Terminal (Ctrl+`):

pwd

What you should see

The status bar at the bottom right shows the Python version (3.14) and .venv. The terminal opens at the bottom of the window, already in the project folder: pwd prints .../smd/ledger, and uv run ledger prints Hello from ledger!.

docs.title: 2. Write the ledger
docs.text:
In VS Code, open src/ledger/__init__.py from the Explorer on the left, and run the commands of this lab in VS Code's terminal. If you can't use VS Code, any text editor works: nano src/ledger/__init__.py in the terminal (Ctrl+O saves, Ctrl+X exits) or TextEdit on macOS in plain-text mode.

Replace the contents of the file with the following, and save it (Cmd+S on macOS, Ctrl+S on Windows). A dot on the file's tab means it has unsaved changes, and uv run only sees what is saved:

"""ledger: balances and spending from a CSV file of transactions."""

import argparse
import csv
from collections import defaultdict
from decimal import Decimal


def read_transactions(path):
    """Reads the CSV file and returns one dict per row, with the amount as a Decimal."""
    with open(path, newline="") as f:
        transactions = list(csv.DictReader(f))
    for t in transactions:
        t["amount"] = Decimal(t["amount"])
    return transactions


def totals_by(transactions, column):
    """Adds up the amounts for each value of `column` (account, category...)."""
    totals = defaultdict(Decimal)
    for t in transactions:
        totals[t[column]] += t["amount"]
    return dict(totals)


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="ledger", description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("command", choices=["balance", "spending"])
    parser.add_argument("file", nargs="?", default="data/transactions.csv")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    transactions = read_transactions(args.file)
    if args.command == "balance":
        for account, total in sorted(totals_by(transactions, "account").items()):
            print(f"{account:<10} {total:>10}")
    else:
        spending = [t for t in transactions if t["amount"] < 0 and t["category"] != "transfer"]
        for category, total in sorted(totals_by(spending, "category").items(), key=lambda item: item[1]):
            print(f"{category:<14} {total:>10}")

Type it rather than pasting it, and notice what the editor does: it completes names (Decim + Tab gives Decimal), shows the documentation of a function when you hover over it, and underlines in red anything it doesn't understand.

What it does:

  • read_transactions uses the standard csv module. DictReader turns each row into a dictionary keyed by the header (t["account"], t["amount"]…). Each amount becomes a Decimal from its string. Step 3 explains why.
  • totals_by adds up the amounts grouped by any column. This is the same idea as s[$2] += $5 in balance.sh.
  • main uses the standard argparse module to read the command line: a command (balance or spending) and an optional file, which defaults to data/transactions.csv.

Run it:

uv run ledger balance
uv run ledger spending
uv run ledger --help
uv run ledger total
What you should see 
checking      3349.10
savings        906.00

The same balances as balance.sh in Lab 2. Then the spending by category, most negative first:

housing          -2850.00
groceries         -797.60
restaurants       -320.09
transport         -135.57
health            -119.70
subscriptions      -77.94

--help prints a usage message that argparse generated for free. ledger total fails with invalid choice: 'total' (choose from 'balance', 'spending'), and echo $? would print 2: a proper error and a proper exit code, unlike the script from Lab 2.

docs.title: 3. Money is not a float
docs.text:
ledger handles money, and the code above stores every amount as a Decimal, not a float. Here is why. Python's float stores numbers in binary, and most decimal fractions, like 0.1, have no exact binary representation, just as 1/3 has no exact decimal one. The error is tiny, but it shows up:

print(0.1 + 0.2)

0.30000000000000004

print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)

False

Adding up many amounts accumulates these errors. These are the payments to a gym in three months, as floats:

print(-39.90 + -39.90 + -39.90)

-119.69999999999999

The standard library's Decimal type stores numbers in decimal, exactly as written, so sums of amounts with two decimals are exact. Create a Decimal from a string, not from a float, or you copy the float's error into it:

from decimal import Decimal

print(Decimal("-39.90") + Decimal("-39.90") + Decimal("-39.90"))

-119.70

print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") == Decimal("0.3"))

True

print(Decimal(0.1))  # created from a float: the binary error is now visible

0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625

In a report, a balance of 3349.0999999999995 looks careless. In a payment system, an amount that is one cent wrong is a reconciliation problem, and comparisons such as balance == 0 can fail when they shouldn't. The rule in financial software is simple: money is never a float. In Python you use Decimal. In databases you use a NUMERIC column (session 7). In some systems amounts are stored as integers in cents.

Now see it in ledger: break it on purpose. In read_transactions, change Decimal(t["amount"]) to float(t["amount"]). In totals_by, change defaultdict(Decimal) to defaultdict(float). Run both commands again:

uv run ledger balance
uv run ledger spending
What you should see 
checking   3349.0999999999995
savings         906.0

and, among the categories, health -119.69999999999999. Same data, same logic, and wrong-looking money. Undo both changes before you continue, and check that uv run ledger balance prints 3349.10 again.

Question. A teammate stores amounts as floats and writes if balance == 0: close_account(). After a deposit of 0.10, a deposit of 0.20 and a withdrawal of 0.30, the account is not closed. Explain why, and show the fix.

Solution

With floats, 0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3 is 5.551115123125783e-17, not 0, because 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 are not exactly representable in binary. The comparison is false and the account stays open with a "balance" of a few hundred-quadrillionths of a euro. With decimals created from strings, Decimal("0.10") + Decimal("0.20") - Decimal("0.30") is exactly Decimal("0.00"), which equals 0, so the comparison works.

docs.title: 4. Add a dependency
docs.text:
Plain columns of text are fine, but a table is easier to read. The rich library draws tables in the terminal. Add it to the project:

uv add rich

Now look at what changed:

grep -A2 "^dependencies" pyproject.toml
uv tree
grep -c "^\[\[package\]\]" uv.lock
What you should see

pyproject.toml now lists one direct dependency with a constraint, such as "rich>=15.0.0". uv tree shows rich and its three transitive dependencies (markdown-it-py, mdurl, pygments). uv.lock has 5 packages: those four plus ledger itself, each with an exact version and file hashes. Your versions may be newer than the ones shown in Dependencies and the lockfile.

Use rich in the spending command. At the top of __init__.py, after from decimal import Decimal, add:

from rich.console import Console
from rich.table import Table

In VS Code, these two lines must not be underlined: if they are, the selected interpreter is not the project's (step 1). Then replace the last two lines of main (the for loop of spending) with:

        table = Table(title="Spending by category")
        table.add_column("Category")
        table.add_column("EUR", justify="right")
        for category, total in sorted(totals_by(spending, "category").items(), key=lambda item: item[1]):
            table.add_row(category, f"{-total:,.2f}")
        Console().print(table)

-total shows spending as positive numbers, and the format ,.2f adds thousands separators and two decimals.

uv run ledger spending
What you should see

docs.title: 5. Isolation
docs.text:
rich is installed in the project's environment, and only there. Check it from outside the project's environment:

python3 -c "import rich"
uv run python -c "import rich; print('rich is here')"
What you should see

The system Python fails with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'rich' (or python3: command not found if your system has none). Through uv run, the import works. Your other projects, and your system, are unaffected by what you install in ledger.

docs.title: 6. Rebuild from the files
docs.text:
The environment is disposable. Delete it and rebuild it:

rm -rf .venv
uv sync
uv run ledger balance

Now simulate a teammate who receives the project. Copy only the files that define it to a new folder, and run it there:

mkdir -p /tmp/ledger-copy
cp -r pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version README.md src data /tmp/ledger-copy/
cd /tmp/ledger-copy
uv run ledger spending
cd ~/smd/ledger
What you should see

After rm -rf .venv, uv sync recreates it and installs the same five packages in well under a second. The packages are in uv's cache, so nothing is downloaded again. In the copy, uv run creates a new environment from the lockfile and prints the same table.

These files are what you will commit to Git in session 5. .venv is not among them.

docs.title: 7. Debug the ledger
docs.text: When a program gives a wrong result, the first reflex is to add print calls, run it again, read the output and remove the print calls. A debugger does the same job without changing the code: it stops the program at the lines you choose, shows every variable at that moment, and lets you run the rest one line at a time.

docs.title: Tell VS Code how to run ledger
docs.text:
VS Code's default debug configuration runs the file open in the editor, without arguments. ledger is a command that needs an argument (spending), so you describe how to run it in a file called .vscode/launch.json.

In the Explorer, click the New File icon next to the project's name, type .vscode/launch.json and press Enter. VS Code creates the folder and the file. Paste this and save:

{
    "version": "0.2.0",
    "configurations": [
        {
            "name": "ledger spending",
            "type": "debugpy",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${workspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/ledger",
            "args": ["spending"],
            "console": "integratedTerminal"
        }
    ]
}
  • "name" is the name you choose from a list when you start debugging.
  • "type": "debugpy" uses the Python Debugger extension.
  • "program" is the ledger command that uv created in .venv/bin in step 4 of Lab 3. ${workspaceFolder} is the project folder. This is what uv run ledger runs: the command imports the ledger package and calls main().
  • "args" are the command-line arguments, the same words you type after uv run ledger.
  • "console": "integratedTerminal" shows the program's output in VS Code's terminal.

docs.title: Stop at a breakpoint
docs.text:
Open src/ledger/__init__.py and find the line inside totals_by that adds up the amounts:

        totals[t[column]] += t["amount"]

Click just to the left of its line number. A red dot appears: that is a breakpoint, a line where the debugger stops before running it.

Open the Run and Debug view (Cmd+Shift+D on macOS, Ctrl+Shift+D on Windows), check that ledger spending is selected at the top, and click the green triangle (or press F5).

What you should see

The program starts and stops at the breakpoint: the line is highlighted in yellow and a toolbar with the debugging buttons appears at the top. On the left:

  • Variables → Locals shows the variables of totals_by at this moment: column is 'category', totals is an empty defaultdict, transactions is a list of 44 transactions (the 56 transactions minus income, interest and transfers), and t is the first of them, the rent:

    {'date': '2026-01-01', 'account': 'checking', 'description': 'Rent', 'category': 'housing', 'amount': Decimal('-950.00')}

  • Call Stack shows how the program got here: main called totals_by. Click main to see its variables (args, transactions, spending), then click totals_by again.

docs.title: Step through the code
docs.text:
The debugging toolbar has six buttons. From left to right, with their keys:

Button Key What it does Continue F5 run until the next breakpoint Step Over F10 run the current line and stop at the next one Step Into F11 go inside the function called on the current line Step Out Shift+F11 finish the current function and stop where it was called Restart Shift+Cmd+F5 / Ctrl+Shift+F5 start again Stop Shift+F5 end the program

On a Mac laptop, the function keys may need Fn, and F11 may show the desktop: use the buttons instead.

Press Step Over twice and watch the Variables panel. The loop runs the highlighted line, goes back to for t in transactions, and stops on the highlighted line again with the next transaction. Values that just changed are highlighted.

Now use the Debug Console, the tab next to the terminal at the bottom. It evaluates any Python expression in the program's current state. Type, one at a time:

t["description"]
dict(totals)
len(transactions)
sum(t["amount"] for t in transactions)
What you should see

After two steps, t is the second transaction (Carrefour, -65.15) and totals contains {'housing': Decimal('-950.00')}. In the Debug Console: 'Carrefour', the same dictionary, 44, and Decimal('-4300.90'), the total spending of the three months.

docs.title: A conditional breakpoint
docs.text:
Stepping through 44 transactions one by one is slow. A conditional breakpoint stops only when an expression is true. Right-click the red dot, choose Edit Breakpoint…, type this expression and press Enter:

t["category"] == "health"

Press Continue. The program runs until the first health transaction. Use Step Over and Continue to follow totals["health"] through the three gym payments.

What you should see

The program stops at the gym membership of 10 January (-39.90). totals has no health key yet. After Step Over it has Decimal('-39.90'). At the next two stops (10 February and 10 March), the total goes to -79.80 and then, after the last step, -119.70.

This is the line where the float version of step 3 produced -119.69999999999999. With Decimal, the sum is exact.

Remove the breakpoint (click the red dot) and press Continue. The program runs to the end, and the table appears in the terminal.

Exercise. Add a second configuration to launch.json that runs ledger balance, and use it to stop in totals_by while it adds up the accounts. What is the value of column this time?

Solution

configurations is a list: add a second object, separated from the first by a comma. Then choose ledger balance from the list at the top of the Run and Debug view.

{
    "version": "0.2.0",
    "configurations": [
        {
            "name": "ledger spending",
            "type": "debugpy",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${workspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/ledger",
            "args": ["spending"],
            "console": "integratedTerminal"
        },
        {
            "name": "ledger balance",
            "type": "debugpy",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${workspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/ledger",
            "args": ["balance"],
            "console": "integratedTerminal"
        }
    ]
}

column is 'account', and transactions has all 56 transactions, because balance doesn't filter them.

docs.title: 8. Lint and format with Ruff
docs.text:
Ruff does two jobs. As a linter, it reads the code without running it and reports problems: names that are not defined, imports that are not used, and many patterns that usually hide a bug. As a formatter, it rewrites the layout of the code (spaces, line breaks, quotes) in one standard style, so that a whole team writes code that looks the same and a code review shows only real changes.

Ruff is a tool for whoever develops the project, not something ledger needs to run. Add it as a development dependency:

uv add --dev ruff
grep -A3 "dependency-groups" pyproject.toml
What you should see 
[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "ruff>=0.17.4",
]

Your version may be newer. Development dependencies go in their own group, separate from dependencies. uv.lock pins Ruff too, so the whole team uses the same version and gets the same results.

docs.title: The linter
docs.text:
Run it on the project:

uv run ruff check

It prints All checks passed!. Now introduce a typo. In totals_by, change for t in transactions: to for t in transaction: and save. Before running anything, look at the editor: Pylance underlines transaction and, when you hover over it, says "transaction" is not defined. Run Ruff, then the program:

uv run ruff check
uv run ledger spending
What you should see

Ruff finds the problem and shows where it is (your line numbers may be different):

F821 Undefined name `transaction`
  --> src/ledger/__init__.py:24:14
   |
22 |     """Adds up the amounts for each value of `column` (account, category...)."""
23 |     totals = defaultdict(Decimal)
24 |     for t in transaction:
   |              ^^^^^^^^^^^
25 |         totals[t[column]] += t["amount"]
26 |     return dict(totals)
   |

Found 1 error.

The program fails with NameError: name 'transaction' is not defined. Did you mean: 'transactions'?. Python only finds the error when it reaches that line. Ruff found it without running anything, and in a big program that line might only run in a case nobody tested.

Fix the typo and check that uv run ruff check prints All checks passed! again.

docs.title: The formatter
docs.text:
Ask Ruff what it would change, without changing anything yet:

uv run ruff format --diff
What you should see

A diff: lines starting with - would be removed, and lines starting with + would be added. Ruff wants to split the two lines of main that are longer than 88 characters:

-        spending = [t for t in transactions if t["amount"] < 0 and t["category"] != "transfer"]
+        spending = [
+            t for t in transactions if t["amount"] < 0 and t["category"] != "transfer"
+        ]

and the same for the for category, total in sorted(...) line.

Now apply it, and check that the program still does the same:

uv run ruff format
uv run ledger spending
What you should see

Ruff reports 1 file reformatted. VS Code shows the new layout of __init__.py, and ledger spending prints the same table as before: a formatter changes how the code looks, never what it does. Run uv run ruff format again: there is nothing left to change.

Ruff has hundreds of rules, and a project chooses which ones to apply in pyproject.toml. We configure them later in the course, when we reorganize ledger into modules. If you want to see Ruff's messages as you type, install the Ruff extension (by Astral) from the Extensions view.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
You have finished the lab when:

  • code . opens ~/smd/ledger in VS Code (on Windows, with WSL: Ubuntu in the bottom-left corner), with .venv as the interpreter;
  • uv run ledger balance prints 3349.10 and 906.00, and uv run ledger spending prints the table;
  • ~/smd/ledger contains uv.lock, and you can explain which files a teammate needs, and why .venv is not one of them;
  • .vscode/launch.json runs ledger spending under the debugger, and you can stop it in totals_by and read t and totals;
  • ruff is a development dependency in pyproject.toml, and uv run ruff check and uv run ruff format --diff report nothing to fix.

Challenge (optional). Add a third command, ledger months, that prints the net change (income minus spending, transfers included) for each month: 2026-01, 2026-02, 2026-03. Hint: t["date"][:7] gives the month of a transaction. You could add it as a key to each transaction and reuse totals_by.
